DashFood is a café pickup ordering system. Customers choose products, check quantities and totals, submit orders and track preparation. Staff manage orders and menu availability. The project uses React/TypeScript, Express and PostgreSQL. Payment takes place at pickup. The prototype contains generated test data; it is not a record of a real café's customers.

Part A — Working prototype (30 points)

A1. End-to-end journeys

Customer: open Menu → check product and price → add to Cart → adjust quantity/remove an item → Place order → view status in My orders. Orders are inserted into PostgreSQL orders and order_items in one transaction. The server reads product prices from products. Staff: log in → open Staff orders → accept New order → mark Ready → complete. Staff may also add/edit/disable menu products. Customer screens read the updated data.

Screenshots below are actual browser captures from the local database-backed prototype. The capture scripts create synthetic verification orders. Full-resolution images and machine-readable check results are in output/evidence.

A1-1. Customer opens menu, sees products, categories and prices.

A1-2. Customer checks quantity and total in the cart before submitting.

A1-3. An order is saved and its number and status appear in My orders.

A1-4. Authenticated staff see incoming orders and can accept them.

A1-5. The customer reads the Ready status after the staff update.

A1-6. Staff can edit product details and disable availability.

A3. Deployment and security

Exact launch instructions are in ИНСТРУКЦИЯ.md. With Docker Desktop open, run bash setup.sh on macOS/Linux or setup.ps1 on Windows, then visit http://localhost:4000. Database state persists in a named Docker volume. Optional Caddy serves https://localhost; a local CA requires explicit trust on the client. Public HTTPS deployment and measured uptime are not claimed.

Passwords are hashed with bcrypt. Staff receive an expiring JWT; admin endpoints check its signature and admin role. A guest request to GET /api/orders returns 401. Parameterised SQL and server validation protect data operations. Prices are retrieved from the database, ignoring browser-supplied totals. Login attempts and JSON body size are limited. Status updates follow New → Preparing → Ready → Completed, with cancellation from New/Preparing. The automated checks demonstrate these boundaries.

The prototype requires a pickup name for each new order and stores it in orders.customer_name. Staff see the name in the authenticated order list; public order lookup omits it. Phone numbers, addresses and payment details are not collected. Cart state and order IDs are stored in the customer's browser. Order IDs are sequential and order lookup exposes item/status information; stronger tracking tokens or account ownership are still required for stronger protection of customer order history. Device/session storage should not be treated as cross-device identity. The Stage 1 / Assignment 3 privacy report and instructor annotations were not provided and must be cross-checked.

Part B — Testing (15 points)

B1. Stage 1 success criteria

The original Stage 1 criteria are checkout in less than 120 seconds, rejection of unavailable products and a working ordering interface at 360 px. Page 8 lists the three priority functions; those are not the success criteria.

The final results supplied by the team are U1: 31 seconds on iPhone/Safari, U2: 24 seconds on Windows/Chrome, and U3: 26 seconds on Android/Chrome. All reported that disabled products were blocked and the interface worked; no problems were reported. Exact viewport widths, dates and assistance were not recorded. These are later Final results, not measurements from the original Stage 2 submission. The full table is in docs/FINAL_TESTING.md.

B2. Usability findings

Three observed user problems and corresponding Nielsen heuristics must be added after external testing. TESTING.md provides the table. Engineering improvements already include visible add-to-cart feedback (visibility of system status), remove/quantity controls (user control and freedom) and validation/unavailable-item handling (error prevention). These are implementation choices, not fabricated participant observations.

Part C — Data analysis (20 points)

C1–C2. Questions and repeatable method

The main table orders is seeded with 120 synthetic records over 14 dates, with related order_items, varying quantities and a repeatable distribution. is_demo=TRUE identifies the seed batch. Manual demos and automated verification add further test orders. Run the exact SQL in docs/ANALYSIS.sql using PostgreSQL psql. GET /api/analytics runs the same GROUP BY/SUM/COUNT queries to populate the product screen.

  1. Which products are ordered most? SUM(order_items.qty), grouped by item name, excluding Cancelled orders; compare the top eight products with horizontal bars.
  2. How does completed revenue change by day? SUM(orders.total), grouped by local date, including only Completed orders; display the latest 14 dates as a line chart.
  3. When is the café busiest? COUNT(orders), grouped by hour in Asia/Qyzylorda; compare hourly demand with horizontal bars. This includes cancelled orders because placing an order still represents an incoming request.

The local date/hour conversion is explicit, so UTC storage does not shift the analysis accidentally. Revenue excludes cancelled and unfinished orders. A cancelled order therefore affects demand counts but does not count as completed revenue.

SQL for question 1:

SELECT i.name, SUM(i.qty) AS items_ordered
FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id
WHERE o.status <> 'Cancelled'
GROUP BY i.name ORDER BY items_ordered DESC LIMIT 8;

SQL for question 2 (reverse the returned rows for chronological plotting):

SELECT to_char(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Qyzylorda',
               'YYYY-MM-DD') AS day, SUM(total) AS revenue_kzt
FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY day ORDER BY day DESC LIMIT 14;

SQL for question 3:

SELECT to_char(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Qyzylorda',
               'HH24:00') AS hour, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders GROUP BY hour ORDER BY hour;

C3–C5. Charts, interpretation and product integration

C5. Insights shows three database-derived charts, summary values and the smart queue estimate.

Each chart has a question as its title, labelled dimensions/units and a source note. The revenue line also provides an expandable table of exact values. Values may change after new test orders; this is expected for a live database. For fixed results add AND is_demo to the source query and record the extraction date.

Interpretation (150–200 words):

We use three charts to look at the order database. Product totals compare the quantities ordered for each menu item, while daily completed revenue shows how order values change across dates. Hourly counts describe when requests enter the system. Each chart answers a different question: popularity concerns preparation quantities, revenue concerns completed sales, and hourly demand concerns staffing. Cancelled orders are excluded from product popularity and revenue, but remain in the incoming-request count. An administrator could use a real version of these results to schedule an additional kitchen worker during a consistently busy period, then check whether preparation delays decrease. In this prototype, however, the main dataset consists of 120 generated orders, supplemented by development verification orders. The seed code creates these patterns. They do not show real customer choices, busy hours or sales. The short date range, limited menu and absence of measured preparation timestamps further restrict conclusions. The charts therefore validate the query and display method, while real operational decisions require representative observations over a longer period.

Part D — Smart technologies and IoT (15 points)

D1. A real food-service example (150–200 words)

Connected refrigerator monitoring is a practical IoT application in food service. Testo Saveris 2 uses temperature probes and Wi-Fi data loggers to monitor refrigerated storage. According to the manufacturer, readings are transmitted through a wireless LAN to the Testo Cloud, where staff can review measurements using an internet-connected device. Configurable alerts inform staff when a limit is exceeded. The manufacturer's food application example specifically discusses monitoring during the processing, storage and sale of food, including restaurant environments. This provides a concrete connection between physical sensors, a network, remote processing and a staff-facing application. A second source, the FDA, explains why reliable refrigerator temperature monitoring matters for food storage and recommends checking conditions with a thermometer. Together these sources support the operational purpose of a connected monitoring system. For DashFood, such monitoring could complement ordering by helping staff detect refrigeration problems before affected ingredients are offered. That proposed connection is our inference, not a claim of an existing integration. One risk is interrupted connectivity: a dashboard that stops receiving updates could otherwise be mistaken for evidence that storage conditions remain normal.

Sources: Testo food application example, Testo Saveris 2-T3, FDA refrigerator thermometers.

D2. Proposed extension: anonymous pickup counter occupancy

DashFood could combine its existing active-order count with an anonymous counter occupancy measurement, helping staff warn customers when pickup is crowded. The physical device is a time-of-flight counter, not a camera. No face images, phone identifiers, names or location histories are needed. A proposed JSON message contains device_id, timestamp, count and sequence number, approximately 100 bytes per reading. One message every 10 seconds is about 8,640 readings / 0.86 MB of raw JSON per day, excluding protocol overhead, retries and indexes. Aggregate by minute, retain detailed data 7 days and aggregates 30 days. These are proposed design choices, not deployed policy.

Four-layer diagram, connected to the existing database:

1 DEVICE / SENSOR
Anonymous time-of-flight pickup counter
    | count + timestamp, every 10 seconds
    v
2 NETWORK
Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3) + HTTPS, per-device credentials
    |
    v
3 PROCESSING / CLOUD
Authenticated ingestion API -> validate/deduplicate -> proposed sensor_readings table
                                                     |
                              existing PostgreSQL <--+--> existing orders table
                                                     |
                              crowd/queue rule <-----+
    |
    v
4 APPLICATION
DashFood staff Insights -> crowd warning / waiting estimate
Customer screen receives an aggregate warning only

The new occupancy/time information can reveal presence patterns even without names. Do not link readings to order IDs, accounts or staff shifts. Authenticate devices, rotate credentials, enforce TLS, limit ingestion rate, reject replayed sequences and impossible counts, restrict raw readings to staff, and display stale-data warnings when updates stop. Update the Assignment 3 privacy analysis before deploying this extension. A real sensor, ingestion route and sensor_readings table are proposed future work, not existing features.

D3. Current smart demonstration

The running Insights screen already demonstrates a software rule on live order data: estimated wait = min(60, 5 + 3 × count(New or Preparing orders)), in minutes. It refreshes every 8 seconds and reacts when staff progress the queue. The screen is explicitly labelled a software simulation with no physical sensor. This is a lightweight smart-rule demonstration, not a claim that the proposed IoT hardware is implemented.
